title: Sigma-algebras
objectives: Check the sigma-algebra axioms and generate the Borel sets.

screens.title: What the report says
screens.prose: A trader sees a die only through a report: "odd" or "even". An event is something she can decide from that report. The grid shades the two groups the report separates.
screens.question: Select all that apply. Which of these events can she decide?

options.text: $\varnothing$
$\Omega$

options.why: You picked an event that splits the even group: the report cannot tell 2 from 4.
You picked a single even number. The report cannot tell 6 from 2 or 4.

hints.text: Which events does 'odd' or 'even' settle?
She can decide any event that is made of whole groups.
Odd, even, neither group, and both groups: four events.

feedback.correct: Four events: odd, even, $\varnothing$ and $\Omega$. Each is made of whole groups.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. An event is decidable when it is a union of whole groups, with no group split.

byKey.one2: {1, 2} takes 2 from the even group and leaves 4 and 6.
byKey.six: {6} takes one number from the even group.

explain.text: The report separates two groups, odd and even. She can decide the events built from whole groups: none, either one, or both. That is $2^2 = 4$ events.

screens.title: A sigma-algebra
screens.prose: The four events form a **sigma-algebra** $\mathcal{F}$ on $\Omega$: a family with three properties. $$\Omega \in \mathcal{F}, \qquad A \in \mathcal{F} \Rightarrow A^c \in \mathcal{F}, \qquad A_1, A_2, \dots \in \mathcal{F} \Rightarrow \bigcup_n A_n \in \mathcal{F}.$$
screens.question: Which properties put $\varnothing$ into the family?

options.text: $\Omega \in \mathcal{F}$ and closure under complements: $\varnothing = \Omega^c$.
$\varnothing$ is a subset of every set, so every family of subsets holds it.
options.why: You used the subset rule. A family of sets need not contain $\varnothing$ unless a property forces it.

options.text: Closure under unions: $\varnothing = \text{odd} \cup \text{even}$, the union of the two events.
options.why: You took the union of odd and even. That union is $\Omega$, not $\varnothing$.

hints.text: Start from the one set the first property gives you.
The second property turns $\Omega$ into another set.
$\Omega^c = \varnothing$.

feedback.correct: $\varnothing = \Omega^c$, so the first two properties give it.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take the complement of $\Omega$.

explain.text: The first property gives $\Omega$ and the second gives its complement, $\varnothing$. Countable unions are the third property: they let a family be built from countably many events at once.

screens.title: A sharper report
screens.prose: A sharper report names the group: $\{1\}$, $\{2, 3\}$ or $\{4, 5, 6\}$. These groups are the **atoms**. Every event she can decide is a union of atoms.
screens.question: How many events can she decide now?

widget.accept: $2^3 = 8$: each atom is in or out
widget.label: Number of events

hints.text: Each event picks some of the three atoms.
For each atom there are two choices: in or out.
$2 \times 2 \times 2 = 8$, counting the empty union.

feedback.correct: 8: each atom is in or out, so $2^3$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the choices: each of the three atoms is in or out.

byKey.three: You counted the atoms. Events are unions of atoms, so there are more.
byKey.seven: You left out $\varnothing$, the union of no atoms.
byKey.six: You counted single atoms and pairs but missed the empty union and the whole space.

explain.text: A union of atoms chooses, for each atom, whether it is in. Three atoms give $2^3 = 8$ events, including $\varnothing$ and $\Omega$.

screens.title: An event as a union of atoms
screens.prose: Same report, same atoms. The event "at most 3" is one the trader can decide.
screens.question: Tap the cells of the event "at most 3".

hints.text: Which numbers are at most 3?
They are 1, 2 and 3.
Atom $\{1\}$ together with atom $\{2, 3\}$.

feedback.correct: Cells 1, 2 and 3: the atoms $\{1\}$ and $\{2, 3\}$ together.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Tap every number up to 3.

byKey.one: You tapped only the first atom. $\{2, 3\}$ is one atom, so it comes in whole.
byKey.r1c1: 1 is at most 3, so it belongs too. Tap all three cells.

explain.text: "At most 3" is $\{1\} \cup \{2, 3\}$, a union of two atoms. That is why the trader can decide it.

screens.title: The sigma-algebra generated by two events
screens.prose: Now start from two events, $A = \{1, 2\}$ and $B = \{2, 3\}$, which overlap. The smallest sigma-algebra holding both has atoms found from $A \cap B$, $A \setminus B$, $B \setminus A$ and the rest.
screens.question: How many events does it hold?

hints.text: Find the atoms first.
$A \cap B = \{2\}$, $A \setminus B = \{1\}$, $B \setminus A = \{3\}$, and the rest is $\{4, 5, 6\}$.
Four atoms give $2^4 = 16$ events.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the atoms, then use $2^{\text{atoms}}$.

byKey.eight: You found three atoms. The rest, $\{4, 5, 6\}$, is a fourth.
byKey.four: You counted the atoms, not the unions of atoms.
byKey.six: Four atoms give $2^4 = 16$ unions, not six.

explain.text: Closing under complements and unions splits the die into $\{1\}$, $\{2\}$, $\{3\}$ and $\{4, 5, 6\}$. A union of atoms is an event, so there are $2^4 = 16$.

screens.title: A family that fails
screens.question: Select all that apply. Which properties fail?

options.text: The complement of $\{1\}$ is missing.
The union $\{1\} \cup \{2\}$ is missing.
$\Omega$ is missing.
options.why: You said $\Omega$ is missing. It is in the list.

options.text: $\varnothing$ is missing.
options.why: You said $\varnothing$ is missing. It is in the list.

hints.text: Check the three properties in turn.
Take the complement of $\{1\}$, then the union of $\{1\}$ and $\{2\}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take a complement and a union of listed sets and see whether they are listed.

byKey.omega: $\Omega$ is the last entry of the list.
byKey.empty: $\varnothing$ is the first entry of the list.

explain.text: $\{1\}^c = \{2, \dots, 6\}$ is not listed, and nor is $\{1, 2\}$. A sigma-algebra holding $\{1\}$ and $\{2\}$ needs both, and many more.

screens.title: Why countable unions
screens.prose: Let $\mathcal{F}$ hold the finite subsets of $\mathbb{N}$ and their complements, the cofinite sets. It is closed under complements and finite unions. Now take the even numbers, one point at a time.
screens.question: Why is $\mathcal{F}$ not a sigma-algebra?

options.text: The evens are a countable union of points, but are neither finite nor cofinite.
A single point such as $\{3\}$ is not in $\mathcal{F}$, so the family is too small.
options.why: You said a single point is missing. A single point is finite, so it is in $\mathcal{F}$.

options.text: The complement of a finite set is not in $\mathcal{F}$, so closure under complements fails.
options.why: You said complements fail. Complements of finite sets are cofinite, so they are in.

options.text: $\mathbb{N}$ itself is not in $\mathcal{F}$, so the first property fails at once.
options.why: You said $\mathbb{N}$ is missing. $\mathbb{N} = \varnothing^c$ is cofinite, so it is in.

hints.text: Which sets does the family contain?
A union of one point at a time is finite at each stage, but the whole union is not.
The evens are infinite and their complement, the odds, is infinite too.

feedback.correct: The evens are a countable union of members, yet neither finite nor cofinite.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for a countable union of members that leaves the family.

byKey.c: Cofinite sets are in $\mathcal{F}$ by definition.

explain.text: Each point is in $\mathcal{F}$ and the evens are the union of those points, taken over a countable list. The evens are infinite, and so are the odds, so neither is finite or cofinite. Closing under finite unions only is too weak.

screens.title: The Borel sets
screens.prose: The **Borel sets** are the sigma-algebra generated by the open intervals. The bars show $[0.4, 0.6]$ as a limit: $\bigcap_n (0.4 - \tfrac1n, 0.6 + \tfrac1n)$, for $n = 4, 8, 16$.
screens.question: Select all that apply. Which of these sets are Borel?

options.text: The closed interval $[0.4, 0.6]$
A single point $\{0.5\}$
The rationals in $[0, 1]$, a countable union of points
The irrationals in $[0, 1]$, the complement of the rationals
The Vitali set $V$ of the last lesson
options.why: You included $V$. It is not Borel: no length can be given to it.

hints.text: Build each set from open intervals using complements and countable unions or intersections.
$\bigcap_n$ of open intervals gives a closed one, and a point is a closed interval of length 0.
Rationals: countable union of points. Irrationals: their complement. $V$ cannot be built this way.

feedback.correct: Four of the five. Only the Vitali set escapes the Borel sets.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Closed intervals, points, countable unions of points and complements are all Borel.

byKey.vit: $V$ is the set with no length. If it were Borel it would have one.

explain.text: An intersection of open intervals gives $[a, b]$, and with $a = b$ a point. A countable union of points is Borel, so $\mathbb{Q}$ is, and so is its complement. The Vitali set is not Borel.

screens.title: Joining two sigma-algebras
screens.prose: Let $\mathcal{A} = \sigma(\{1\})$ be the sigma-algebra generated by $\{1\}$, and $\mathcal{B} = \sigma(\{2\})$ the one generated by $\{2\}$. A colleague merges the two lists into one family $\mathcal{A} \cup \mathcal{B}$.
screens.question: How many sets does the merged family hold?

hints.text: List each sigma-algebra first.
$\mathcal{A} = \{\varnothing, \{1\}, \{2, \dots, 6\}, \Omega\}$, and $\mathcal{B}$ likewise for $\{2\}$.
$\varnothing$ and $\Omega$ sit in both lists, so $4 + 4 - 2 = 6$.

feedback.correct: 6. And the merged family is still not a sigma-algebra: $\{1\} \cup \{2\} = \{1, 2\}$ is in neither list.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count $\varnothing$ and $\Omega$ once.

byKey.eight: You added 4 and 4. The empty set and the whole space are in both lists.
byKey.four: You counted one list. The other adds two sets of its own.

explain.text: Each list holds four sets, and the two lists share $\varnothing$ and $\Omega$. That is six sets. The union $\{1, 2\}$ is in neither list, so a union of sigma-algebras is generally not one.

screens.title: Where the union breaks
screens.prose: The merged family $\mathcal{A} \cup \mathcal{B}$ from the last screen holds six sets. We check the three properties in turn.
screens.question: Which line shows it is not a sigma-algebra?

options.text: $\{1\} \in \mathcal{A}$ and $\{2\} \in \mathcal{B}$, but $\{1, 2\}$ is in neither, so unions fail.
$\Omega \notin \mathcal{A} \cup \mathcal{B}$, so the first property fails for the union.
options.why: You said $\Omega$ is missing. It is in both lists.

options.text: $\{1\}^c \notin \mathcal{A} \cup \mathcal{B}$, so closure under complements fails for the union.
options.why: You said a complement is missing. $\{1\}^c$ is in $\mathcal{A}$ and $\{2\}^c$ is in $\mathcal{B}$.

options.text: Each of $\mathcal{A}$ and $\mathcal{B}$ is a sigma-algebra, so their union must be one.
options.why: You assumed a union of sigma-algebras is one. This example is a counterexample.

hints.text: Check complements, then unions of one set from each list.
Take $\{1\}$ from the first list and $\{2\}$ from the second.
$\{1, 2\}$ is neither in $\mathcal{A}$ nor in $\mathcal{B}$.

feedback.correct: Unions fail. A sigma-algebra generated by both sets must also hold $\{1, 2\}$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take one set from each list and join them.

byKey.c: Each list is closed under complements by itself.

explain.text: The family is closed under complements, since each list is. It fails for unions that mix the lists. We need $\sigma(\mathcal{A} \cup \mathcal{B})$, which has 8 sets.

screens.title: Generating a sigma-algebra in code
screens.prose: On a finite $\Omega$ a countable union is a finite union. Write `generate(omega, events)`, closing a list of events under complements and unions, and `is_sigma_algebra(omega, sets)`, which checks the three properties.
screens.question: Complete both functions.

widget.how: Check runs 10 hidden tests on a die. Five test generate (sizes 4, 8, 16 and 2, and one member). Five test is_sigma_algebra, including the merged family of the trap.

hints.text: Start from $\varnothing$, $\Omega$ and the given events, then keep adding.
Add the complement of every set and the union of every pair, and repeat until nothing new appears.
`is_sigma_algebra`: check `omega` is in the family, then every complement and every pairwise union.

feedback.correct: Right. Closure finds 4, 8 and 16 events, and the merged family fails the check.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Return frozensets and repeat the closure until the family stops growing.

explain.text: `generate` closes the family under complements and pairwise unions until it stops growing. On a finite space that is a sigma-algebra. `is_sigma_algebra` checks the same three properties directly.

screens.title: A risk report
screens.prose: A risk system reports daily P&L in three bands. They are a loss over £1m, between, and a gain over £1m. The bands are the atoms of a sigma-algebra. The desk has a limit on losses over £2m.
screens.question: Can the report decide whether the limit was breached?

options.text: No. "Loss over £2m" is not a union of bands: it cuts the first band.
Yes. A loss over £2m is also a loss over £1m, so the first band decides it.
options.why: You used the first band. It also holds losses between £1m and £2m, so it cannot settle the limit.

options.text: Yes. The report holds $2^3 = 8$ events, so every event is decidable.
options.why: You counted 8 events and assumed all events are in it. "Loss over £2m" is not one of the 8.

options.text: Only on days when the P&L is a gain.
options.why: You split by sign. On a loss day the report cannot say how big the loss was.

hints.text: Is "loss over £2m" a union of the three bands?
The first band holds every loss over £1m, including small ones.
Losses between £1m and £2m sit in the same band as losses above £2m, so the report cannot separate them.

feedback.correct: No. A limit needs an event the sigma-algebra holds, and this one is finer than the atoms.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask whether the limit event is a union of the three bands.

byKey.b: The first band is too coarse for the limit.
byKey.c: Eight events does not mean every event.
byKey.d: The band cannot size the loss.

explain.text: The sigma-algebra has 3 atoms and $2^3 = 8$ events. "Loss over £2m" is a strict part of the first atom, so it is not one of them. Reporting is a choice of sigma-algebra, and it fixes which limits can be checked.

ideas: A sigma-algebra holds $\Omega$ and is closed under complements and countable unions. It is the family of events you can decide.
Atoms are the finest groups the family separates. With $k$ atoms there are $2^k$ events, each a union of atoms.
The Borel sets are generated by open intervals. They hold intervals, points, the rationals and the irrationals, but not the Vitali set.

formula.name: Sigma-algebra
formula.note: Closed under complements and countable unions.

summary.trap: A union of two sigma-algebras is usually not one: it misses unions across the two lists.

quiz.prose: A die has 6 outcomes. The largest sigma-algebra holds every subset.
quiz.question: How many events is that?

feedback.correct: 64: every outcome is in or out, so $2^6$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each of the six outcomes is in or out of a subset.

explain.text: Every subset is an event, and there are $2^6 = 64$ subsets. The smallest sigma-algebra, $\{\varnothing, \Omega\}$, knows nothing and holds 2 events.

quiz.question: Which event must it also hold?

options.why: You split the atom $\{2, 3\}$. Nothing in the family separates 2 from 3.
You took one point of the atom $\{2, 3\}$ with $\{1\}$. The atom stays whole.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take unions and complements of the two given sets.

quiz.prose: The irrationals in $[0, 1]$ are the complement of the rationals in $[0, 1]$.
quiz.question: Why are they Borel?

options.text: They are the complement of the rationals, a countable union of Borel points.
They contain no open interval, and every set like that is Borel.
options.why: You used a property of the set that is unrelated to being Borel.

options.text: They are uncountable, and every uncountable set of reals is Borel.
options.why: You used the size. Some uncountable sets, such as the Vitali set, are not Borel.

feedback.correct: A countable union, then a complement.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Build the set from points using the sigma-algebra rules.

explain.text: Each point is Borel, so the rationals, a countable union of points, are Borel. The Borel sets are closed under complements, so the irrationals are Borel.

quiz.prose: On a die, $\sigma(\{1\}, \{2\})$ is generated by two disjoint events.
quiz.question: How many events does it hold?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The atoms here are $\{1\}$, $\{2\}$ and the rest.

explain.text: The events $\{1\}$ and $\{2\}$ are disjoint, so they are atoms, and the remaining outcomes form a third. Three atoms give $2^3 = 8$ events.
